name: Turkish
intro: Turkish is agglutinative: suffixes express relationships that English often expresses with separate words. Learn vowel harmony, consonant alternations and suffix order, then recognise words by their structure. Stress has lexical and grammatical exceptions. Standard Turkish is the principal model; professional writing needs precise nominal and participial constructions.

foundation.name: Turkish
notes: Turkish distinguishes dotless ı from dotted i, including capitals I and İ. Q, W and X are not core Turkish letters. c is /dʒ/, ç /tʃ/, ş /ʃ/, j /ʒ/. ğ generally modifies adjoining vowels rather than having one fixed consonant sound.

Back vowels a/ı/o/u contrast with front e/i/ö/ü. A two-way suffix alternates a/e; a four-way suffix often alternates ı/i/u/ü, following backness and rounding. Harmony is a productive guide, with lexical exceptions.

Stress is often final but place names, loans and some suffixes differ. A final voiceless consonant can select a voiceless suffix consonant: kitapta. Some stems voice before a vowel suffix: kitap → kitabı.
building: ev → evler → evlerimiz → evlerimizde = house → houses → our houses → in our houses. Plural, possession and case follow a fixed sequence.
ev + ler → evler; kitap + lar → kitaplar. ev + de → evde; kitap + ta → kitapta. Both vowel and consonant harmony matter.
Türkçe öğreniyorum. = I am learning Turkish. Türkçe öğrenmiyorum. = I am not learning Turkish. Negation, tense/aspect and person are expressed within the verb.

sections.title: Vowel harmony and noun morphology
sections.explanation: Many suffixes use two-way or four-way vowel harmony. Back/front and rounded/unrounded vowels guide selection. Evler and kitaplar show plural harmony. Accusative often marks a specific/identifiable direct object; an unmarked object can be indefinite. Possession and case combine in an ordered sequence. Buffer consonants and changes such as kitap/kitabı require lexical pattern learning.
examples: book / the book as a specific object
Ev + plural + first-person plural possession + locative.
exercises: Segment evlerimizde.
Ev-ler-imiz-de: house-plural-our-in.
Why should every direct object not automatically receive accusative?
Specificity/identifiability and construction determine marking; bare indefinite objects occur.

sections.title: Verb tense, evidentiality and negation
sections.explanation: Turkish distinguishes forms including -DI past and -mIş, often associated with inference or reported information. Their interpretation depends on context and narrative conventions. Progressive -(I)yor, future -(y)AcAk and aorist forms have distinct uses. Negation is usually built into the verb through -mA before other suffixes. Person marking differs across tense patterns.
examples: Specific object plus -DI past and first-person marking.
Apparently/he or she has written the report.
-mIş can present reported/inferred information; context determines nuance.
exercises: Is -mIş merely the English perfect tense?
No. Evidential and narrative meanings can be central.
Translate I am not reading.
Okumuyorum. Negative vowel interaction occurs before progressive and person suffixes.

sections.title: Cases, postpositions and predicates
sections.explanation: Dative -(y)A, locative -DA, ablative -DAn and genitive -(n)In express governed relationships. Postpositions can require a particular case. Nominal predicates take person marking or copular constructions without an English-style verb in every present clause. Değil negates many nominal predicates; yok denies existence or possession in suitable patterns.
examples: I need information on this topic.
A possession/need construction rather than English subject-verb mapping.
exercises: Distinguish değil and yok.
Değil denies a predicate relation; yok states absence/nonexistence in its relevant construction.
What belongs with a postposition entry?
Required case, meaning, usage and a full example.

sections.title: Participles and nominalised clauses
sections.explanation: Turkish frequently places a clause-like modifier before its noun. -(y)An commonly forms subject-related modifiers, while -DIK and -(y)AcAk with possessive marking support other clause relations. Okuduğum kitap means the book I read; the first-person relationship is inside the modifier. Nominalised clauses can take case and act as arguments. Long words must be segmented without assuming every suffix keeps one constant English meaning.
examples: Participial/nominal modifier with first-person possessive marking.
I know that he/she came/has come
exercises: Locate the head of okuduğum kitap.
Kitap. The modifier precedes it.
Why does geldiğini need context for person interpretation?
Pronouns are often omitted, and morphology must be read with the discourse and nominalisation pattern.

sections.title: Professional reading and polite requests
sections.explanation:
Teaching passage: Sonuçlar iki etken arasında bir ilişki olduğunu gösteriyor. Ancak bir etkenin diğerine neden olduğunu kanıtlamıyor. Sonucu değerlendirirken araştırmanın koşullarını dikkate almak gerekir.
Translation: The results show that there is a relationship between two factors. However, they do not prove that one causes the other. The study conditions must be considered when evaluating the conclusion.
examples: Ability plus polite plural/person question pattern.
exercises: What does olduğunu do in the passage?
It nominalises a subordinate proposition so it can be the object of showing or proving.
Write a professional summary.
Preserve evidential strength, suffix harmony and clause relationships.

rules.title: Pronouns
rules.explanation: Subject pronouns can be omitted when verbal endings identify the subject. O does not distinguish he/she/it. Case suffixes create object and other pronoun forms with some irregular stems.

examples.translation: She ate the bread.
I work for McDonald's.

examples.native: Boston'da yaşayan tek Kanadalı ben değilim.
examples.translation: I'm not the only Canadian living in Boston.

rules.title: Demonstratives
rules.explanation: Bu/şu/o encode distinctions of reference and distance. Their pronoun inflections use a buffer n in relevant forms. Context, not English this/that alone, determines the best choice.

examples.native: Neden herkes için yeterli yiyeceğimiz yok ? Bu öğleden sonra alışverişe gittiğinizi sanıyordum.
examples.translation: Why don't we have enough food for everyone? I thought you went shopping this afternoon.
We can make this work.

examples.native: Bu, bu bölgede bugüne kadar en iyi deniz ürünleri restoranıdır.
examples.translation: This is by far the best seafood restaurant in this area.

rules.title: Plural nouns
rules.explanation: Plural -lar/-ler follows two-way vowel harmony. Numerals commonly precede an unmarked counted noun, so do not add a plural suffix automatically after every number.

examples.translation: People say that I look like Tom.

examples.native: Arıcılar balı toplamak için peteği kaldırdılar.
examples.translation: Beekeepers remove the honeycomb to collect the honey.

examples.native: Tom anneler gününde annesine bir buket çiçek gönderdi.
examples.translation: Tom sent a bouquet of flowers to his mother on Mother's Day.

rules.title: Location suffix
rules.explanation: Locative -DA combines vowel harmony and consonant assimilation. The capital notation stands for alternatives, not a written capital suffix. Lexical words can end similarly; inspect their stem.

examples.translation: Do we have to do all that?
What would you like to have for dinner?

examples.native: Hafta boyunca daha az kalabalık görünüyor.
examples.translation: It seems less crowded during the week.

rules.title: Source suffix
rules.explanation: Ablative -DAn expresses many source/from relations and governed complements. A final voiceless stem consonant commonly selects t. Meaning depends on the governing phrase.

examples.translation: I've been coughing since this morning.
Never let a crisis go to waste.
Study harder from now on.

rules.title: Accusative objects
rules.explanation: Accusative commonly marks a specific/definite direct object. The suffix follows four-way harmony with a buffer y after a vowel in applicable nouns. Bare objects have different interpretations and positions.

examples.native: Onları bulmak için sana ihtiyacım var.
examples.translation: I need you to find them.
You shouldn't have followed me.

examples.native: Tom ona onu kimin söylediğini hatırlamıyor.
examples.translation: Tom doesn't remember who told him that.

rules.title: Dative direction
rules.explanation: Dative -A marks many destinations and recipients. Ben/sen have irregular bana/sana forms. English to maps to several Turkish constructions, so learn verb government.

examples.translation: Don't you ever touch me again.
Give me time to relax.
I can't give it to them.

rules.title: Possession and genitive
rules.explanation: A genitive possessor commonly pairs with a possessive suffix on the possessed noun. Benim kitabım means my book. A possessive relationship is not expressed just by juxtaposing two unchanged nouns.

examples.native: Onun tekrar olmasına izin vermeyeceğine güveniyorum.
examples.translation: I trust you won't let that happen again.
I own a horse.
I've got company.

rules.title: Progressive verbs
rules.explanation: The -Iyor construction marks a progressive/current pattern and takes personal endings. Vowel interactions can change the stem surface. Learn negative -mIyor separately from a mechanical -ma + ıyor spelling.

examples.translation: I know who got the prize.
Are you still having fun?
The principal wants to talk to you.

rules.title: Past forms
rules.explanation: The -DI past uses vowel/consonant harmony and personal endings. Its evidential orientation contrasts with common -mIş forms, though discourse can refine the contrast.

examples.translation: Jane made an angry gesture.
I got here about thirty minutes ago.

examples.native: Mary kardeşine yeni bir elbise yaptı.
examples.translation: Mary made her sister a new dress.

rules.title: Reported/evidential forms
rules.explanation: The -mIş series often presents information as inferred, discovered or reported. It is not exclusively hearsay. Possessive and verbal morphology may add further endings.

examples.translation: We wouldn't have gone if it had rained.

examples.native: Sen muhtemelen daha önce bu parka hiç gelmemiş Boston'daki tek kişisin.
examples.translation: You're probably the only person in Boston who has never been to this park before.

examples.native: Büyükanne bütün aileyi buz kesilmiş bırakarak öldü.
examples.translation: Grandmother died, leaving the whole family stunned.

rules.title: Future forms
rules.explanation: Future -AcAk harmonises and combines with person endings. Intervocalic k can become ğ before a vowel suffix. The same form can also participate in a nominal or adjective construction.

examples.translation: Her mother will continue to work.
Tom will never allow you to go.
How will you go to Boston?

rules.title: Negation and absence
rules.explanation: Değil negates many non-verbal predicates; yok expresses absence; hayır is a response no. Verbal negation usually belongs inside the verb. Hiç often works with a negative construction.

examples.translation: Tom isn't very secretive.

examples.native: Tüm nedenimizi izlemek için yeterli gücümüz yok.
examples.translation: We do not have enough strength to follow our reason completely.

examples.native: Tom iyi ama yeterince iyi değil.
examples.translation: Tom's good, but not good enough.

rules.title: Question particle
rules.explanation: The question particle is written separately and follows harmony. It attaches in position to the focused element; personal endings can follow it. A question word does not normally need an extra question particle.

examples.translation: Do you like squash soup?
Are you still not convinced?
Have you guys seen the news?

rules.title: Question words
rules.explanation: Location, destination and source have different question forms. Question words take relevant case morphology. Context and focus govern their placement.

examples.translation: Wow! What a big box!

examples.native: Ne zaman Boston'a gitsek Tom'la kalırız.
examples.translation: We stay with Tom whenever we go to Boston.
When will we go back?

rules.title: Postpositions
rules.explanation: Postpositions follow a complement and may require a particular case. Bana göre uses dative; benden sonra uses ablative. Learn the whole governed phrase.

examples.native: Diğer üç kişi özel övgü için seçildi.
examples.translation: Three other people were singled out for special praise.
We're done for today.
Tom had no desire to go out with Mary.

rules.title: Conditions
rules.explanation: Conditional suffix -sA and related forms encode different time and reality relationships. Eğer can introduce a condition but is not necessary in every conditional sentence.

examples.native: Eğer isteseydi Tom Mary'ye yardım edebilirdi.
examples.translation: Tom could help Mary if he wanted to.

examples.native: Eğer Tom Mary'ye yardım edebiliyorsa, neden John'a da yardım edemiyor?
examples.translation: If Tom can help Mary, why can't he help John, too?

examples.native: Bir şeye ihtiyacın olursa beni ara.
examples.translation: Call me if you need anything.

rules.title: Clause linking
rules.explanation: Connectors mark cause, contrast and coordination. Turkish also uses suffix-based non-finite clauses extensively; do not assume every English connector needs a separate Turkish word.

examples.native: Tom ve arkadaşı plastik kılıçlarla düello ediyorlardı.
examples.translation: Tom and his friend were duelling with plastic swords.
Tom and Mary used to be married to each other.

examples.native: Dikiş dikmeyi bıraktı ve biraz çay içti.
examples.translation: She stopped sewing and had some tea.

rules.title: Participles and nominal clauses
rules.explanation: Participles modify nouns before them; nominalised clauses can take possessive and case endings. The form records relationships that English often expresses in a separate relative/content clause.

examples.translation: I assumed Tom was your boyfriend.

examples.native: Daha fazla zamana ihtiyacın olduğunu söyledin.
examples.translation: You said you needed more time.

examples.native: Tom başka herkesten daha akıllı olduğunu düşünüyordu.
examples.translation: Tom thought he was smarter than anybody else.

rules.title: Ability, necessity and courtesy
rules.explanation: Lütfen marks a polite request; belki limits certainty; gerek/lazım often express necessity. Daha/en participate in comparison and degree. Use the full construction to identify their role.

examples.translation: Please behave honestly.
He is the most valuable player in our team.
Japanese is harder than English.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
